speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, on December 10 the Leader of the Opposition asked me a question on the subject of Soviet imperialism and consideration of this problem by the United Nations.
As I have stated on several occasions, my objective has been that the Canadian government should through international consultation secure sufficient international support to focus United Nations attention squarely on the unsatisfactory conditions in the Soviet empire. This government deeply deplores Soviet Russia's hypocritical position on colonial questions arising in the United Nations, especially in the light of the Soviet union's own record of subjugation and tyranny over races and nations. Our view is that the provisions of the charter of the declaration on human rights and of the declaration on colonial independence are universal in their application.
I had hoped that the consultations which have been going on throughout the year and
also during the current session of the general assembly would serve to mobilize sufficient support for a resolution in regard to the question of Soviet colonialism. At a time when the concern of a great many members of the United Nations is principally engaged in respect of colonial questions affecting Africa, the moment for the successful presentation of a resolution aimed at the situation in the Soviet empire has not yet come.
Nevertheless there is a growing awareness that a Soviet imperialistic system does exist and that the United Nations cannot ignore it. The forthright condemnation of Soviet imperialism which the Canadian representative, the hon. member for Queens (Mr. Mac-quarrie), made in the general assembly on November 23 was intended to bring home to all members of the United Nations the essential fact of Soviet domination of subject peoples.
I assure the house that it will not be long before this resolution can be introduced. Every effort is being made to secure the widest possible general support and as soon as we are in a position to be reasonably assured of substantial and, indeed, more than a bare majority support, the resolution which we undertook to introduce will be brought before the assembly.

speechtext: ['Order. The house will now revert to the business that was interrupted by the reversion to motions for the purpose of permitting the Minister of Trade and Commerce to make his announcement.', 'The house in committee of supply, Mr. Chown in the chair.']

When 1 rose immediately before the close of proceedings last evening I indicated to the committee that I wished to address a few remarks on this occasion on Canada's foreign trade policy. In bringing this question forward at this time I should like to associate myself with the remarks made by other members of this party with regard to the fact we are being asked now to vote the tenth of twelve instalments of expenditures totalling approximately $6 billion by the federal government for the current fiscal year. I deplore the fact that an important question like Canada's trade has not been brought before the house before this time, so that the members of this house have not had an opportunity to consider in detail the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce or to examine more fully with representatives of the government the trade policies which the government is following at this time.
I submit to the committee that the question of Canada's foreign trade relationships is perhaps one of the most critical questions arising in Canadian public affairs today, and one of the questions which should commend itself to the attention of hon. members of this house. Perhaps the best point at which to commence this discussion is to make reference to the
actions of the government itself in this field. We have heard from the Minister of Trade and Commerce and his assistant, as well as various other spokesmen, and we have seen evidence in the press and elsewhere in recent weeks about the government's principal action in this field, a program known as "Operation world markets".
May I hasten to say that members on this side of the house can only commend the minister and the department for the effort being made in connection with that program. The program is really designed for the purpose of disseminating more widely information on trade prospects and trade possibilities, and indicating to both Canadian manufacturers and foreign purchasers the opportunity for trade with Canada. In fact an even more extensive compliment has been paid to this program, not so much by members on this side of the house but by the Ontario department of economics and development and particularly the minister of that provincial department. He has emulated the federal minister's policy with Ontario's trade crusade.
I should like to address a few remarks to the committee on the question of Ontario's trade crusade, particularly with a view to bringing to the committee's attention the fact that one aspect at least of that crusade represents an invasion by the provincial government into the federal field. It represents a usurpation by the province of Ontario of the responsibility of the minister in the field of trade.
Hon. members cannot have escaped being exposed to the extensive advertising campaign which has been conducted by the Ontario government in radio, television and the press during recent weeks. The principal purpose of that particular advertising is to persuade the Ontario consumer to discriminate in his buying decisions between domestic and foreign products where quality and price are equal, purely on the basis of national production. I submit to the committee that this is discrimination, a boycotting of the products of our trading partners, and that as such it involves Canada in a serious derogation from its international legal obligations with regard to trade.
In support of that argument I should like to refer the committee to the opinion of Sir H. Lauterpacht, a recognized authority on international law in this generation and formerly one of the British judges of the international court of justice, as outlined in an article entitled "Boycott in International Relations", which may be found in volume 14 of the British Year Book of International Law, page 125 and more particularly at page 131. The writer makes particular

reference to commercial treaties entered into between nations, similar to the kind entered into by Canada for foreign trade relations whereby access to the Canadian market is assured for foreign products, and he makes the following observation:
The commercial treaty obviously implies that the state cannot prohibit generally the importation and sale of goods coming from the territory of the other contracting party. But does it mean that it may not exhort its citizens not to buy the goods of the state with which it has a commercial treaty and that it must not place its governmental departments at the disposal of the boycott propaganda? ... If a state promises to another state to grant to its merchants "complete protection and security for their commerce" then it ill becomes it to exhort its citizens to suppress such commerce and to make its governmental services available for propaganda to this end. By no stretch of interpretation could such an attitude be squared with the undertaking to confer upon foreign merchants the same "privileges, liberties and favours" as are enjoyed by the state's own citizens.
On the basis of that authority, Mr. Chairman, I submit that the Ontario trade crusade, or that part of it which is directed to discriminating between foreign and domestic products purely on the basis of nationality, involves the federal government in a breach, on the international scale, of Canada's foreign trade obligations.
I would also like to bring to the attention of the committee at this time a further legal objection to that aspect of the Ontario trade crusade. Under the constitution of Canada, the British North America Act, and more particularly under the provisions of section 91(2) of that statute, it is provided that the regulation of trade and commerce is the exclusive responsibility of the government of Canada. The general words of that section have been more particularly elaborated upon by the courts in various discussions through the years, and it has been conclusively established with respect to import and export trade that the government of Canada, not the provinces, has sole jurisdiction with regard to legislative and executive measures affecting the import and export trade.
In support of that proposition I would like to refer the committee to the margarine reference in the Supreme Court of Canada in re the validity a section of the Dairy Industry Act which may be found in 1949, Supreme Court Reports, page 1, and more particularly in the remarks of Mr. Justice Rand at page 53. Mr. Justice Rand, in upholding the fact that the federal government has exclusive jurisdiction over imports, made reference to the particular import restriction contained in the federal statute there in question:
Such scope of action is clearly necessary to the nation's jurisdiction over trade with other states. Only parliament can deal with foreign commerce:
Interim Supply
provincial power cannot in any mode, aspect, or degree govern it: and it would be anomalous that the jurisdiction to which regulation is committed, which alone can act, and which in this segment of trade is in substance sovereign, should be powerless to employ such an ordinary measure of control.
I therefore make the observation that this government, and more particularly the Minister of Trade and Commerce, should take an early opportunity to make representations to his colleague who represents the provincial riding of Riverdale that this aspect of the Ontario trade crusade program which relates to restriction of the free circulation of imports in the province of Ontario is in derogation of federal government responsibility in law, and is also in excess of the provincial government's power in trade and commerce. Indeed, the failure of the federal government and of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to take action in this regard is an astonishing failure. In fact just the other day, on Tuesday, the minister spoke in this house, and I quote his words as recorded at page 2527 of Hansard:
I am always interested to hear any observation of Mr. Macaulay because in representing his government he is doing the same kind of job for the producers of Ontario as this government is doing for the producers of Canada.
My submission is that it is not Mr. Macaulay's right or duty to do the identical kind of job. It is rather the exclusive duty of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to make regulations with regard to the export and import trade. The minister has failed to carry out that duty. It is all the more interesting to note that as a result of the initiative which Mr. Macaulay has shown he now appears to have taken over the trade and commerce of this country altogether. In answer to a question yesterday it was indicated that the Minister of Trade and Commerce had complied with an invitation from Mr. Macaulay summoning him to attend a meeting on trade and commerce next January.
Reference to the Ontario trade crusade assists me in introducing a second aspect, namely the limitations of a trade policy which is based entirely on an advertising campaign. It is all very well to provide the public with trade information and intelligence as to the availability of Canadian products, but at the same time there must be some assurance that the products available are capable of competing in international trade. In this connection I should like to quote what the Canadian consumer has to say for he, perhaps better than any other, can judge the effectiveness of Canadian products in this regard. I intend to refer to a number of letters which appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail

Interim Supply
in connection with the Ontario trade crusade. The first appeared on November 26, 1962. I quote:
"Who is the world's greatest importer?'' I am asked every morning over the radio. And I am not kept in suspense, but told right away that I am- that is, the Canadian public is the greatest importer-and I am urged to buy fewer imported goods and more Canadian ones.
With this in mind, I inspected the Christmas gifts I had bought the night before. I found that X had purchased:
One necktie-made in Switzerland; one ladies' scarf-made in France; one pair slippers-made in England; one pair gloves-made in Japan.
Frankly, I was dismayed. So I set out to buy some more gifts, this time inspecting the place of origin before buying. Specifically, I was looking for a key chain (found that it was made in Italy) and a plastic cosmetic case (found that it was made in Sweden). The only Canadian gifts I could have purchased were coasters with flying Canada geese on them, or a leather bookmark-Indian handcraft-but even there sometimes you discover a tag saying "Made in Japan".
I ask again: "Who is the world's greatest importer?" The answer is obvious. It is not the public, certainly. If the public wishes to buy, it has no choice but to buy imported goods, as these are the ones offered on the counter.
So, may I suggest, instead of wasting time and money on this radio announcement day by day, let's rather ask those responsible:
"Why don't you sell more Canadian goods?"
That letter invited a second which appeared on December 1 as follows:
For six Christmases now we have played the "Made in Canada" game in our search for gifts to send to Britain. If anything we are even more frustrated than Mrs. A. E. Vayk (Who is the Greatest Importer?)-November 28, by the Ontario government's fanciful commercials.
So far, this is what we have bought: Writing paper and envelopes (made in Sweden)-the alternatives were made in Britain or the United States; phonograph records (made in Canada by a British owned company); wooden bowl (made in Canada)-surpassed in quality by U.S. products which we decided not to buy; books (all printed in the United States); nylon stockings (made in the United States).
It's the old story: the consumer will buy Canadian if well made products are available at the right price. My answer to the Ontario government is nuts (from Brazil).

I wonder if I might raise a point of order. The hon. member has almost succeeded in proving to our satisfaction that trade is under federal not provincial jurisdiction. Now he is carrying on with an attack on the Ontario government's trade plan. It seems to me that the very logic of the argument he used in the first part of his statement makes the remarks he is now addressing to the committee out of order. If not I would like to ask you, Mr. Chairman, whether we can embark on comments along the same lines, because I should certainly like to say many things about the Ontario government's trade plan.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for Port Arthur for bringing this point to
[Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale).I
the attention of the committee. The legal argument presented so ably by the hon. gentleman is one of relativity. It must be related to a particular item in the resolution, which he can probably do now for the benefit of hon. members of the committee. Apart from that I would have intervened had he continued in the provincial field, dwelling too heavily on the policies of that government.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: My suggestion concerning the point raised by the hon. member for Port Arthur is that clearly the hon. member from Rosedale is denouncing the activities of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and saying why he is opposed to them, and he is opposing the policies of the Ontario minister inasmuch as these relate to them. I think it is interesting for the country to note that the Liberal party is opposed to this policy.

I thank the parliamentary secretary, and I think I can anticipate the concern of the hon. member for Port Arthur. The crux of my argument was that there is an inadequacy, as indicated by the material I have quoted, in the Canadian products offered in this purchasing field. I was going on to suggest specific measures which this federal government could take to encourage Canadian manufacturers to remedy that inadequacy. I am suggesting that the improvement of Canadian products cannot be brought about by any fiat of the Canadian government. The ultimate decision must be taken in the private field.
In the session of 1960-61 this parliament included the activities of the design centre in a statute known as the National Design Council Act, which endowed that council with certain powers in respect to design in Canada. I suggest to the minister that the activities of the national design council should be expanded, and that in particular the council should set up a procedure whereby it would carry out examinations from time to time of all the products offered on the Canadian market in a particular field.
What I am suggesting is action of the kind carried out in the United States by the consumers' union, the results of which are published in the Consumers Reports. There would be an evaluation of the functional quality, design and workmanship of the products being placed on the Canadian market, both domestic and foreign, and the results could be made available to Canadian manufacturers so they might determine whether their products were competitive and the manner in which they could be improved. One benefit of such a study would be an indication, in a manner which has not been possible under previous arrangements and under the

jurisdiction of the tariff board, of what the real interest of the domestic consumer is. If it turns out that there are no competitive domestic products offered, the argument becomes impressive that whatever tariff charges exist should be dropped.
But the principal question arising in the trade field at this time surely concerns the action which Canada should be taking with regard to foreign trade agreements. For the first time in a generation the log jam of structural arrangements in the international economy is being broken. We are now, and will be for the next two or three years, in a period of flux. In that time we will have an opportunity to make for ourselves trade arrangements which could assure the Canadian manufacturing industry and other Canadian producers effective participation in world trade.
I would like to enunciate a number of principles which I think should govern the government in its trade policy, and more particularly a number of realities which the Canadian government and the Canadian public should bear in mind regarding their forthcoming trade negotiations.
The first of these principles is this. We should recognize that not only should the British be sympathetic to our position but we should show some sympathy for theirs. Their current negotiations with the European economic community are nothing less than negotiations for the continuing survival of their community. The British, in exactly the same way as we have, have inherited from the past an economic system and a societal structure which may not be too directly related to the political realities of the present. No doubt all hon. members of the house over the years have approved the political decisions whereby the British government gave up control of its overseas colonies and thereby gave up control of economic matters in those countries. In the same way we must recognize that to sustain the same population and to maintain the standard of living for the British community we must permit them, and indeed assist them, to establish an equally advantageous trading relationship so they can be assured of continued prosperity.
The second major reality is that the arguments of the high protection group, and the argument in particular that Canadian prosperity can be assured by a general raising of tariffs, is no longer valid. This is so not only because of the fact-and I think we must recognize this-that the Canadian consumer will not tolerate a lower standard of living
Interim Supply
which would be the result of greater protection, but also in an increasingly interdependent world our trading partners will not tolerate this sort of action.
Third, we must bear in mind that tariff negotiations have all the aspects of a primitive bargain; that in going into these negotiations we must be prepared to give in order to get.
We must also bear in mind that Canada is at a not inconsiderable disadvantage in the sense that with our domestic market of only 19 million souls we do not have as advantageous a plum to offer as the European economic community which, including the United Kingdom, has a population of 225 million people. In other words we wish to secure access to that very much larger market for a limited number of products, but we can only offer a very much smaller market for a wider range of products. We must bear in mind the fact that it is not so much a matter of our being able to blast our way into world markets, or negotiate our way in, but that we do not have that much to offer in the way of an advantageous market for, particularly, the producers in the European economic community.
The fourth reality I think we should bear in mind is that the tariff reductions which must come as a result of the multilateral negotiations will have a severe effect on Canadian industry. Indeed, in some industries the effect may be well nigh fatal. This is the necessary cost of expanding to make our products competitive on a world basis, and this is the kind of problem that we face. Hon. members will find in title III of the U.S. trade expansion act of 1962 very elaborate provisions for adjustment assistance to both employers and employees in industries which have been affected by adverse import competition.
The fifth and final reality, Mr. Chairman, is that we must in the interval prior to negotiations, govern our trade policies in such a way that we enter those trade negotiations, which require nimble footwork, not on a limping basis but with full ability to assure our trading partners that we will accord them fair treatment and also live up to our obligations. I suggest that in very recent years, perhaps even more so in the past five years, this government has failed to discharge its international obligations with respect to foreign trade, first by acting in direct contravention of our obligations under the general agreement on tariffs and trade and imposing the tariff surcharges, and second by the boycott campaign which has been carried on by the Ontario provincial government. We must be prepared to act fairly in

the agreements arising out of these trade negotiations, and we must be prepared to win the confidence of the other negotiators by indicating that we are prepared to live up to our existing agreements.

was interviewing students and faculty members at Canadian universities about the political activities that students and faculty members were engaging in. We raised this matter on Tuesday with the Minister of Justice. It was raised by three members of this party, and the minister did not give us an answer. He said there had been no complaints. However, we take the view that it is not a question of whether the minister has had any complaints. Members of this party have had complaints, and we should like to know whether in fact the R.C.M.P. is being instructed by the minister to carry out this sort of activity.
We raised the matter again yesterday on the orders of the day. We asked the minister whether in fact the R.C.M.P. was interviewing students and faculty members at Canadian universities for the purpose of getting them to inform on one another with regard to their political activities, and once again we failed to get any response from the minister. We take the view that the minister's silence is significant and bolsters the information which we have received from a number of sources; and we should like to have from the minister an assurance that this sort of thing will not continue but will stop at once.
This, of course, is something which it seems to me cannot be blamed on the R.C.M.P. The R.C.M.P. is simply acting under instructions from governmental authorities, and it is the government's responsibility if in fact the R.C.M.P. is interviewing students and faculty members at universities for the purpose of discovering what political activity is taking place on our campuses and who is taking part in such political activities. This is something which the members of this party wish to see stopped. We would welcome from the minister an assurance that in fact it is going to stop.
We believe it is wrong for the R.C.M.P. to engage in this activity. We believe that universities ought to be places where young men and women and faculty members may speak their minds, about politics and ideas and do so freely, without members of the national police force coming on to their campuses and asking them questions about the political activities of their friends, their teachers or their fellow students. We believe that otherwise no university can be truly free or can really spawn the kind of discussion that produces new ideas or new concepts or the kind of thinking which must be in the van of any civilization that is moving forward. For the R.C.M.P. to engage in interrogating students and faculty members about their

political activities and about the political activities of their colleagues is to engage in something which can only breed suspicion and fear at Canadian universities. If this continues the effect, of course, will be to curb freedom of thought discussion, and the development of ideas.
If subversion is taking place or if the government is fearful that subversion is taking place in this country, may I make this suggestion; and when I speak of subversion let me make it perfectly clear what I mean. If the ministry is concerned about violations of the Criminal Code we suggest there is a way in which to go about the matter. There is a way in which to carry out effective police work, and there are ways in which to carry out what will only turn out to be quite ineffectual police work. There are ways of enforcing the laws of this country. We in this party suggest that one way which has nothing to do with law enforcement, which has nothing to do with protecting this nation against violations of the Criminal Code and other federal and provincial statutes, is by having police officers interrogating students and lecturers at Canadian universities for any purpose.
We suggest that this sort of thing, emulating the methods of the police state, must come to an end. We suggest that this sort of thing constitutes a misguided attempt to protect freedom and can only result in destroying freedom. -or in real fact are foolish or stupid people. Our society, our civilization, rests on human rights and fundamental freedoms, and these exist for the purpose of facilitating the development of our culture, primarily to assist us in the search for truth, to enable us to move forward. If we destroy these human rights and fundamental freedoms, if we curb freedom of thought, freedom of speech, freedom of discussion-the freedom to generate new ideas, we are doing a disservice not only to the people who are concerned about

Surely we can permit ideas from every quarter to contend in the market place of ideas. That was the view of a great liberal, John Stuart Mill, who said in his famous essay on freedom, in effect "Let these ideas clash in the market place of ideas". If the ideas which we espouse are the ideas which are most consistent with the truth and which lead us toward the truth, then they will emerge triumphant in the clash of ideas. If our beliefs are not tested they can have no firm basis. They can only be tested by exposing them to ideas opposed to them.

For some reason which I have never heard satisfactorily explained, a great many of our young people in the western world begin to sneer at the principles of democracy somewhere around the age of 16 and they keep it up for the next five or six years. Mr. Todgham said to combat the problem businessmen should encourage youth to form junior achievement clubs, miniature companies with shares.

Mr. Speaker, conversations were held yesterday and today with a United States delegation concerning trade in oil and petroleum products between Canada and the United States. The United States delegation was led by His Excellency Walton Butter-worth, the ambassador of the United States, and included Assistant Secretary Griffith Johnson of the United States department of state and Mr. John Kelly, assistant secretary of the department of the interior. The discussions were useful and informative and provided an opportunity for the United States representatives to explain the President's recent proclamation concerning the mandatory control system for importations of oil into the United States, and the amendments which have been introduced into this system.
The two delegations noted that no change has been made in the overland exemption for oil which permits sales of Canadian oil in United States markets without licensing. The continuing importance to the security of the two countries of the availability of continental supplies was recognized. The two delegations discussed estimated trade in oil and oil products in the first six months of 1963. It was agreed that a further meeting would be held to review the situation and to discuss the future growth of trade in the light of the mutual interests of the two countries.

Mr. Chairman, almost three months have passed since I, like many new members, first took my seat in this parliament. Like most new members, I approached my new role with a preconceived idea of what parliament was all about. I had based this conception of parliament possibly on the many years I have spent in civic administration. I resolved to approach my duties without a very rigid party outlook on the affairs of parliament and a willingness to admit some merit in the present government. I came here, for instance, with sincere admiration for the performance of the previous minister of justice in so far as his efforts in the area of penal reform were concerned. I came here in appreciation of the winter works program which the Tory government had instituted, because the city of Verdun has taken full advantage of this program. I can realize how many other communities across the country have found it to their advantage.
I came here also, Mr. Chairman, fully aware of the problems that face this great country of ours. Like many Canadians not too well versed in financial problems I realized the pegging of the dollar indicated something drastically wrong with the economy of the country. I realized the necessity for the introduction of the austerity program. I realized, too, that the last few years of the history of this world have been very momentous ones, a period when flying around the world has become commonplace. I thought possibly this Tory government could be partly excused if they had not had an opportunity of adjusting

to the times. I was even willing to realize that by the fortunes of war this government had been given a second chance to rectify its errors by introducing some of the plans that were so badly needed to get Canada's economy rolling again.
Almost three months have passed, Mr. Chairman, and those three months have convinced me that this government cannot or will not face reality; it will not provide the leadership and the legislation that this country needs. The lackadaisical, almost callous manner with which interim supply is treated makes a mockery of the fundamental rights of parliament. This is the tenth request for interim supply and it indicates the reluctance of this government to bring to the attention of the house the specific reasons for which this money is needed. In the three months that we have sat here, only the estimates of the Department of Agriculture have been discussed in any detail. Once again we are being asked to grant this government vast sums of money without being accorded the opportunity of protecting the interests of the people of Canada.
There may be a precedent for such a procedure, Mr. Chairman but I, for one, being used to the businesslike administration of civic affairs, cannot comprehend how a government can come back month after month and ask for money without indicating to parliament how this money is to be spent.

In the light of that I would like to say a few words on the Columbia power treaty. Our newspapers and parliamentarians have cried out for a cessation of this trend and for a cessation to the constant outflow of Canadian profits into American industry; yet the government refuses to debate what is possibly the largest sellout of our natural resources in the history of our young nation.
I am the first to admit I know very little about the Columbia treaty, but many years ago I learned that the difference between a wise man and a fool is that the wise man knows how little he really knows. So long as there are great Canadians like General McNaughton who express misgivings and opinions that this treaty is not in the best interests of Canada, I feel parliament is duty bound to discuss the matter at the first opportunity, if only to convince the people of Canada that it is a good treaty. Certainly I cannot understand the reluctance of the government to discuss fully the merits of the treaty, if it is indeed good for the country; and in reviewing it we ought to bring to the attention of the house the fact that the day has long passed when we should sell our birthright and the birthright of future generations for immediate gain.

Certainly, in business both big and small everyone must periodically give an account of their financial position. Certainly, small business men render accounts periodically to government agencies which have been set up to receive them. Why is the government shirking it responsibility? Our government has a responsibility in this regard. How long is it going to shirk this responsibility and make a mockery of parliament? How much longer can this government expect to borrow and spend money without rendering an account to the Canadian people?
In closing I feel that this great nation will yet reach the heights predicted for it by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, for underlying the fumbling and inefficiency of the present government are the Canadian people who have the power to remedy the situation. This government has made a serious mistake in not taking full advantage of its second chance to rectify its errors, and I am sure the Canadian people will do it for them.

To talk, as the hon. member for Verdun has talked, about there being some sort of lack of action on the part of the government just defies understanding in the English language. It is the sort of talk people from other parts of the world are inclined to use when they say black is white, red is blue, and so on. It seems to me that in this House of Commons we have to get down to using the English language as it is spoken in this country, otherwise the people simply will not pay any attention to any of the politicians here. I have heard over and over again the dreary and trumped up charges that characterize the speeches of the Leader of the Opposition, epitomized by the unreality which has been the hallmark of all Liberal discussions on the question of national affairs during these last eight months, this complete unreality in debate, unrealistic forays introduced into the discussions of our national affairs. And that isn't peanuts, as my hon. friend from Rosthern says. We only have to look at the use that is made of some of these tremendous projects. Mr. Chairman, I should like to turn to the record in Ontario to see what use Ontario is making of this great scheme. What use did Ontario make of this great scheme? I noticed that one of the hon. members who spoke earlier was jeering at the Ontario government. He asked what use the Ontario government is making TMr. Jones.]
of this federal government scheme. May I say that, as of November 14, they are taking no less than $186,654,000 worth of federal money to help construct technical and vocational training schools. This scheme is open to any province. Any province can put forward to the federal government a scheme for approval by the Minister of Labour. The size of the contribution of the federal government to any particular province does not depend on the federal government but rather on the province. If the province asks for these schools, they will get them. The federal government is contributing $186 million worth of technical training schools in Ontario alone. That is just the federal government's share. It represents a tremendous advancement in technical schools.
I should like to give some of the figures with regard to the situation just in the Toronto region alone. In Toronto the total estimated cost of the approved plan for the technical and vocational training capital projects is $30,239,806, of which the federal government's share is $21,161,417. In this technical training school program Toronto alone is getting more from the federal government than is any other individual province in Canada.
I think one of the arguments that has been put forward in the course of this debate and in past times is that this government plans its projects in some bits and pieces manner. What a false charge that is. One thinks of the situation in Toronto. One thinks of how we have been building in Toronto a great marshalling yard so that the manufacturers and labourers in Toronto can get their produce out of that area and into the world markets and into the markets of Canada and the United States. One thinks of that $143 million marshalling yard. They are getting a $40 million or $50 million airport in Malton at the edge of Toronto, and this $21 million technical and vocational training school project. All these things are working together to increase the productivity of that area.
It is a great and co-ordinated project, particularly when you consider the actions which have been taken in bringing down the value of the Canadian dollar in order to give our exporters an advantage in world markets so that exporters not only in Toronto but in all parts of the country, and particularly in the agricultural and primary producing areas, have a good chance to get their exports into the world markets on favourable terms. This is a great and co-ordinated plan, a great and co-ordinated project, and it deserves commendation.
Certainly it may be the fact that not too many Conservative members were elected

from Toronto, but that is not the fault of those three cabinet ministers and the other members who represented Toronto previously, as they certainly worked in the best interests of their area and of Canada in promoting these great schemes.
These technical and vocational training school projects which I just mentioned are ones that deserve the special commendation of all people in this country, no matter from what part of the house they may come. I would ask for special support for this project. If we can induce the people of this country to make the proper use of these schools in order to get the training they need, so as to upgrade Canadian skills and Canadian abilities to the end that Canadians can compete in the matter of skills with the other nations of the world, then we shall be doing a great service to the people of Canada. This is a matter which should be beyond partisan consideration. It is the greatest project for technical training that has ever been devised in the western world in recent times.
It would seem to me that we hardly need to refer to some of the remarks which have been made in this House of Commons during the course of this debate in order to substantiate further the charge I have made that the speeches in the house are getting so far from English usage that they become almost meaningless. I wish to refer to comment which appeared in an editorial in the Ottawa Journal of December 13, and in which the writer deals with this problem or one aspect of it. The editorial is entitled, "The Tyranny of Words", and it reads in parts as follows:
Somebody some years ago wrote a book on "The Tyranny of Words".
We think of it as we read a charge by the Toronto Star that Senator Wallace McCutcheon, recently appointed by the government to advise on implementation of the Glassco report, has become an "economic czar".
Now a czar, a term applied to Russian emperors, means a Caesar, somebody whose word is law, or who is above the law, responsible only to himself; all-powerful.
Has Senator McCutcheon become that?
The editorial goes on to answer that question, "Hardly"-as, of course, Senator McCutcheon is obliged to submit to the cabinet any proposals he makes. The editorial finishes up in this manner:
Actually, our political vocabularies have become shot through with words and phrases that are utterly meaningless, phrases and terms that represent nothing more than an alien hangover from Europe.
An example is an article in the current print of Maclean's on the Conservative party, telling how the party has a "right," or "left" and "centre". Which is complete nonsense. One might write of a "left" and "right" and "centre" in the politics

of Italy or France or Germany; applied to the politics of Canada, or to a party in Canada, it is meaningless gibberish.
Then the editorial concludes as follows:
Finding one's way through the jungle of existing Canadian politics is hard enough at best; to further confuse it with a fog of alien terms and phrases sins against clarity-and sometimes against honesty.
That is my plea today, namely that we get back to discussing the affairs of this nation in terms of fact; that we do not characterize boom in this country as doom; that we do not characterize programs for progress as programs of regression; that we do not make such silly statements as the one which was made by the hon. member for Rosedale earlier, namely that the minister of economic affairs in Ontario had taken over the post of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in the federal government. Silly and irresponsible remarks of this sort do not do anything to raise the dignity and level of debate in parliament. That is my plea today. During the course of the rest of the life of this parliament I hope that we can get back to discussing our nation's affairs in a manner of which we can be proud and in a way which will make the Canadian people proud of us.

Mr. Chairman, I rise in this debate to renew a plea made by the Leader of the Opposition as recently as October 26 for a special committee of the house on defence policy, and reiterated by him on November 7. The background against which this plea is made is, I suggest, a sombre one. Time and again the opposition has sought from the government statements of defence policy. Such requests appear to have fallen on deaf ears. Time and again questions have been asked with respect to specific aspects of our defence efforts and answers have not been provided. The questions have been parried with, I regret, very great persistence. Attempts to secure a general defence debate in the house have likewise been unsuccessful. In such a situation how can the people of Canada find out what the defence policy of Canada is, in so far as the government is responsible for it?

I wonder whether the hon. member would answer a question. I should like to ask him whether the confusion that exists has been a factor in leading his colleague and defence spokesman for his party to the decision he has made sort of unilaterally and on his own.

Mr. Chairman, the question endeavours to impute motives and ascribe intentions to members of the Liberal party. I win let the statement of the hon. member for Trinity stand on its own feet.
How can the public ascertain what the defence policy of the Canadian government is? There have been scattered statements by high ranking officers who have retired, but unfortunately on a number of occasions these statements have tended to conflict. It is difficult to get a consensus from them. There has also been a series of attempts by ministers of the crown in a vague general way to deliver an assurance not to worry, that everything is all for the best. This, however, fails quite naturally to assuage the worries and perplexities that the present situation inflicts on the public.

The lack not only of a policy but perhaps even of an intention to enunciate a policy is evident from the last white paper issued by the present Minister of National Defence which is dated May 1, 1961, about 18 months ago. Previous white papers on defence had started off as an introductory theme, with a number of paragraphs under the heading "Defence Policy," in which some attempt was made to enunciate a coherent whole and into which the armed forces programs would fit. The present Minister of National Defence has, however, studiously avoided even using the word "policy" in his white paper and has plunged from the first page into an outline of the activities, rather than the ideas, of the various armed forces and the defence research board. I suggest that if the government either is unable or unwilling, but in any event declines to provide leadership to the people of Canada in this important field, it then remains for those of us elsewhere and those other Canadians who can, to ascertain as best they may what the facts are and to attempt to discuss them in an intelligent way. I would suggest to the hon. member who just asked the question, that is precisely what the hon. member for Trinity was endeavouring to do. In the circumstances, he appears to have been better informed than the Minister of National Defence has been willing to admit himself to have been informed, and to have drawn what one can only conclude were logical and serious conclusions from his information.
In a broader field it is agreed, I think, by all in Canada that in defence matters it is impossible for Canada to go it alone. There is universal agreement on the necessity, in our circumstances, to form part of a system of collective security. I do not think there is any dispute, at least I have never heard it seriously argued, that adherence to a system of collective security is anything but necessary for Canada. One of the advantages to be derived from forming part of such a system is that it does provide for each of the members thereof an opportunity to choose and play a role which is appropriate to the circumstances of that member. It would be hoped that in any such system, each of the members would play its fair and appropriate part. Perhaps the only practical way of measuring what should be an appropriate scale of effort is to examine defence budgets expressed in terms of currency, to examine the size of the defence budget.
Our defence budget has remained substantially constant over the past ten years and, for the year 1961, accounted for 5.7 per cent of our national income. Amongst our NATO allies this occupies roughly the middle range

of scales of effort. It does represent a standing of fourth in the list in respect of the size and scale of our defence effort over the years and appears to have represented a fair share. But it must be recognized that any substantial change in our defence budget, either up or down but more particularly any decrease of significance, would be interpreted by our allies as a significant change in our military and political relationships to them. The defence budget, and in particular its size is significant in our relationship with our allies and a sudden change, except in the event of substantial change in the international climate, would give rise to some further serious questions.
I might try to look briefly at what the threat is to Canada in the present circumstances. This would appear to reside largely in the Soviet union and its satellite countries. The military threat posed by the Soviet union to North America is in the form of both nuclear and conventional forces. The conventional forces would be, for attacking this continent, so unecomomical and so expensive to put into operation and sustain, that it is unlikely to enter the mind of a strategist that this would be an appropriate choice to make. There does, however, remain the possibility of the employment of nuclear weapons.
The Soviet union is known to possess a number-not very large-of submarines capable of launching nuclear weapons, a number of intercontinental ballistic missiles with nuclear warheads, and a very large number of high speed, long range, high altitude aircraft. I think military experts are in general agreement that the Soviet union now possesses a sufficient volume of these nuclear weapons that, used in combination, it would be possible in spite of any efforts we may make on this continent, to visit on North America a weight of attack which would cause organized society, as we know it, to cease to exist. For technological and financial reasons combined, I suggest that North America cannot provide a scale of defence which can effectively prevent the Soviet union from landing on this country sufficient nuclear weapons to cause virtual annihilation.
Fortunately for us, perhaps, there is in the hands of the United States an arsenal which is capable of doing precisely the same thing to the Soviet union in spite of any effort now or in contemplation by the Soviet union to prevent this. This, then, is described as the nuclear stalemate. However, we in North America have expressed as an article of faith, the conviction that under no circumstances will the western forces, and in particular those in North America, initiate one of these annihilating attacks. In order, then, for us

to be effective militarily against the Soviet union, it must clearly be possible for us to survive in North America the launching of a massive attack on this country and still be able to reply so as to visit annihilation on the Soviet union.
From Canada?
I said North America.

I would hope the hon. member who spoke from his seat would try to be patient for a little while, come out of his parish and look a little farther afield.

He did not say
that.

Before this outbreak, I suggested we had undertaken and firmly persuaded ourselves that we would never make the first attack. We would, therefore, have to have the capacity, in the event of a massive attack being launched on North America, to reply. This, in current terms, is described as the second strike capability. To do this we must have the means of ensuring that, should there be launched a massive attack on this country, the nuclear riposte of the United States would not be neutralized. If it is apparent to the Soviet union, and clearly apparent, that a massive attack launched on North America will invite a successful massive retaliation on them, it is then reasonable to assume that reasonable men in the Kremlin, not wishing a successful retaliation, will never in the first place launch a massive attack.
Canada does not form part of the retaliatory force. We do, however, have a role in trying to ensure that the retaliatory force, the second strike capability, in fact has a second strike capability; and to examine how we achieve this one has to look briefly at the nuclear forces of the United States. These are composed of Polaris missiles carried in nuclear submarines, intercontinental ballistic missiles stored for operation in hardened or reinforced concrete covered bases, and a very large force of bomber aircraft under the control of strategic air command.
The nuclear submarines bearing nuclear missiles, by their very nature, by their ability to hide under the oceans, are in themselves their own protection and by themselves can remain invulnerable. The intercontinental ballistic missiles must rely for their invulnerability on the thickness and depth of the

concrete, and on the possible inaccuracies of an attack. They are safe from all except a direct hit. The bomber aircraft of strategic air command are extremely vulnerable to attack when they are on the ground. If, however, they get up into the air they then become invulnerable, so the problem then is to organize ourselves so that in the event of attack warning can be given to these aircraft in sufficient time to allow them to take off, become airborne and consequently be invulnerable. This then in the role or function in which Canada can be of assistance.
Warning of an attack is now provided by means of very powerful, very large radar systems installed in Alaska, Greenland and the United Kingdom which have the ability to detect and record immediately ballistic missiles from the Soviet union very shortly after the moment of launching. If these can be detected at the time of departure an amount of warning can then be transmitted to continental United States which will enable the aircraft of strategic air command to become airborne before the arrival of these missiles, and if the strategic aircraft become airborne before the arrival of missiles, no useful purpose would be served in endeavouring to attack the airfields from which they have taken off.
In so far as attacks by enemy aircraft are concerned there is a system of warning lines of which everyone is well aware, the distant early warning line, the mid-Canada line and the Pine Tree line. These also provide sufficient warning of an attack to enable, in their present state of alert, strategic aircraft to get off the ground before they can be destroyed.
This then is the function that we can and do perform in safeguarding the second strike capability, in making the retaliatory forces of the United States invulnerable to an attack and consequently able to survive an announced massive attack and be able to retaliate after that. The theory is, and I think it is a sound one, that so long as we have second strike capability it would be disastrous and completely unprofitable for an aggressor to visit an attack on North America.
There is, however, one other possibility, and that is a sneak attack on the strategic air command bases. This could be attempted by placing in North American air space a sufficient number of nuclear carrying vehicles to be able simultaneously, and without any warning, to drop their nuclear bombs on the airfields before SAC aircraft could take off. To do this it would be necessary to introduce unbeknownst to us, an estimated 200 aircraft, or perhaps less than 200.

To prevent this is I suggest one of the principal day to day functions of NORAD, and it is achieved in this fashion. The perimeter of North America is divided into a series of sectors or zones called air defence zones. Any aircraft flying into, through or from these zones is required to file a flight plan. The flight plan is fed into a computer in Colorado Springs, and immediately on taking off in flight each of these aircraft is tracked by radar. The report on this tracking is then fed into the computer and when the report and the flight plan match, the aircraft can be assumed to be identified. When they do not match there is a demand on the local authorities to identify the tracked aircraft.
This is done by radio-telephone, by wireless means, or if all else fails by sending up one of the NORAD aircraft to establish contact and make a visual identification. Because this is done 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, it is quite apparent that it is impossible-and I stress impossible-for a number of hostile, clandestine aircraft secretly to get into North American air space within range of these SAC airfields without North American air defence having knowledge of them. So, if it is apparent to a possible aggressor that they cannot proceed to do their jobs in secret, that they must of necessity be discovered before they can achieve their purposes, then there is no sense whatever in attempting an attack in that manner, and the fact of our being able to identify every aircraft flying through the perimeter of North America makes a sneak attack impossible to achieve on a secret basis and consequently not worthwhile attempting.
If such an attempt were made it would of necessity fail, not by reason of the incoming aircraft being destroyed before delivering their bombs, but because of discovery, the target they were seeking on the ground, the SAC aircraft, would have left by the time they arrived.
There is one further aspect of this warning system and that is the possibility of the positioning in North American waters, on the east and west coasts, of nuclear propelled or even conventional submarines with nuclear missiles therein. For warning against this and the detection of such operations we rely mostly on naval craft, sea-going waterborne craft, with very limited means of detection indeed. There is not nearly, in this area, the assurance there is against the possibility of clandestine operations that we have in respect of clandestine operations in the air. This problem of the detection of possibly hostile undersea craft is a serious one and a problem to which we should probably give the highest priority in terms of military and intellectual effort.

If, then, in respect of the North American defence we have an adequate system of warning and we have the ability to guarantee a retaliatory force with a second strike capability, then there will be little likelihood that short of virtual insanity there will ever be either an attack by surprise or a deliberate attack launched on North America. Essentially the elements in this are a retaliatory force capable of dealing a knockout blow to the Soviet union regardless of any defensive measures which might be taken and the means to render this retaliatory force invulnerable to an attempt to destroy it before it could become operative. This, I suggest, we now have. In this Canada has a role to play and is playing that role.
In Europe the situation is somewhat different. In the fifties the NATO concept was that if one could place along the perimeter of the Soviet a screen sufficient to cause an aggressor to concentrate substantial numbers of forces in order to penetrate it there would be no possibility of a lightning stroke as a result of which the Soviets might overrun western Europe without resistance and, once installed, be difficult to remove. This temptation would be removed by a sufficient depth of screen to compel any break-through to be made on a fairly large scale. With this screen in position it was the declared intention of the United States that serious endeavours to penetrate it would be regarded as deliberate aggression on all the NATO countries and would be replied to immediately by the launching upon the Soviet union of the retaliatory force from the United States.
Latterly, however, it has come to be recognized that this all or nothing philosophy does give rise to serious dangers. There is the ever present danger that the Soviet union might conclude that the United States would be unwilling in the face of a light provocation to launch the one and only reply of a total nuclear attack. This has led to efforts by the United States recently to have established under NATO a force which in itself would be sufficient to accept and deal with serious and heavier forms of aggression. This is the reason for the initiative currently being taken in Paris.

I am grateful to the committee and particularly to the hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam.
I was saying that these considerations led the United States to attempt to increase the size, scope and potential of the military forces in Europe. The new concept provides not only the NATO countries in Europe but the free world in general with a wider range of choice as to responses to be made in the event of aggression in Europe, which may start more likely as a consequence of error or by miscalculation than as a consequence of deliberate intention. In this system of collective security which I have endeavoured to outline, Canada, as I have suggested, can have a choice of roles to play. With the strengthening of NATO forces in Europe there is manifestly required a vast array of military weapons systems and of military roles. We, as a member of this collective security organization, have not only the freedom but we also have the duty to contribute a role or function, or series of functions, appropriate to our situation.
If I have anything useful to say today it is to try to give the committee some suggestions as to what might be the considerations which would affect our choice of role.
First, we should seek military functions which call for highly trained military personnel and require a relatively high degree of technical skill. This is appropriate for the long service, volunteer military personnel we have. It is also appropriate to the product of our defence industry in North America and it is appropriate to the standard of living we enjoy and the standard of the products we make. It is more useful to us and to our allies if advantage is taken of the fact that we in Canada can produce highly trained personnel in both a technical and a military sense who are equipped by reason of a voluntary long term engagement to serve continuously over a period of time. Our soldiers, sailors and airmen now enjoy a reputation of being, if not the best equipped, at least the best trained in the world. I think it is highly desirable that we should see this kind of reputation continued. Second, we should seek a military function which corresponds to an essential-and I emphasize

the word "essential"-military purpose within the alliance. In so far as can be foreseen this military function should be likely to continue to be essential.
There is the danger, as we see it here today, of adopting a function or a role which is non-essential in the general scheme of things and will possibly fall by the wayside. We must adopt a role or a function which is essential for the moment and which also is not going to fade out in a short time. We, for financial and other reasons, cannot afford the luxury of plunging into expensive military training, expensive military organization and hardware for a very short period of time. We have to try and take a long look at the problem and engage in the kind of function which, as I say, is not only essential for the moment but is likely to continue to be essential for some time to come. This does not mean that the weaponry, the hardware which this role or function will require will not change. It must, of necessity. But we want to try and ensure that the role or function of itself is not likely to disappear.
Third, we should seek military functions which are geared more closely to our industrial economy and which, certainly in large part, lend themselves to research activities within our industrial complex. Then perhaps, more than has been the case in the past, this would serve to provide in respect of our scientific community, a counter attraction to the vast attractions of the United States. The number of highly educated scientists we have lost over the past few years has been, to say the least, distressing. It has been very serious indeed for Canada. A military function which is geared to our industrial economy would also serve in some measure to alleviate the serious balance of payments problem we are now facing and which in my view are likely to continue to face for some time to come. No means should be overlooked which would be useful in tackling this major economic problem which we face.
Fourth, we should seek a military function which does not impede or run counter to the possibility of useful diplomatic initiatives which Canada can, and if it can, should, undertake in the world. We have, or had in the past at least, a reputation and an influence in this area which far outweighed the size of our population and the size of our economic efforts. We should under no circumstances allow ourselves to be put in a position where our military functions and roles are such that we are estopped from putting forward in the diplomatic field a constructive, productive effort on behalf of peace.
Fifth-and I think this will be understood and almost goes without saying for all Canadians-such functions and roles should be

adopted not unilaterally by ourselves but in the light of the fullest discussion and agreement with our partners. We must not become isolationist in this field, even in approach; we should not become unilateral. We are members of a coalition; we are members of a partnership and we should behave like partners. We ask for consultation from our other partners. We must and should be equally prepared to provide consultation to them on what we intend to do.
I would suggest that perhaps consideration of the criteria I have suggested, when applied to our apparent dilemma in North America, might shed some light on this problem.
In respect of NORAD we perform two functions. One of them corresponds to all the tests I have outlined and the other does not. The military task of identification and warning which is NORAD's main task does correspond to the criteria I have just outlined. The function of aircraft interception and destruction-more particularly aircraft destruction- with nuclear weapons, does not correspond, and it is because this particular function into which we appear in the past three years to have rather drifted does not correspond, that we are faced with the spectacle-
That is better than bird watching.

Mr. Chairman, I shall be very brief for I only have a few remarks to make before we approve the interim supply for the current month.
Ten weeks have already gone by since the beginning of the session and we have had all sorts of discussions. We have heard talks on the speech from the throne and we have also seen the old line parties indulging in petty politics, which is just like them.
Which party are you talking about?

The one my hon. friend belongs to.

as well as the setting up of an economic development board for the Atlantic area, etc.

Later on, we are asked in this house to set up more advisory boards which, I believe, shall meet the same fate.
We expected the government to put forward legislative measures likely to solve the serious economic problems of today.
We expected the government to come forward with a great program of public works so as to cope with the present unemployment.
We also expected that the government would bring forward an amendment to the Income Tax Act, and that it would have, above all, increased the basic exemption for Canadians, especially for workers who have been claiming, these last years, an increase in the basic exemption from income tax, that is already too heavy for them to carry. We also thought that the government would amend the Family Allowances Act by bringing under its scope the students from 16 to 20 years and by increasing these allowances to keep up with the increase in the cost of living.
We had thought also that the government would increase the old age security pensions to meet the cost of living and grant them to people 65 and over.
But we have found the government very slow in legislating in those fields.
We had also thought that we could resume the debate on the bill respecting the creation of an advisory council on manpower adjustment, but I doubt very much that we can do it before the Christmas recess. There again, we are dealing with a consultative service.
I am of the opinion that the first step the government should take to stem unemployment is to create new jobs.
Mr. Chairman, we are in favour of the establishment of consultative services, but we are of the opinion that, first and foremost, it is up to the government to create new jobs throughout the country in order to alleviate the present unemployment situation.

grant interest-free loans to municipalities wishing to carry out extensive public works programs, would be an illogical step.

In this connection, Mr. Chairman, allow me to quote from Einstein's book. This scientist is considered as the greatest mathematician in the world and his teachings are accepted by all economists.
I quote excerpts from the book entitled "How I see the world" by Einstein, which was edited by "Les Editions Flammarion". Einstein said:
Production and purchasing power.
The gold standard has, in my opinion, one great shortcoming: when there is a tightening up of this metal supply, it automatically entails a contraction of credit and of legal tender in circulation. Price and salary cannot adjust quite fast enough to such contractions.
The natural means to overcome those drawbacks are in my opinion the following:
I am still quoting Einstein:
The legal and gradual decrease, along trade lines of working hours in order to suppress unemployment, together with the fixing of a minimum salary, to control the purchasing power of the masses, in accordance with the available production of goods:
Control of the money supply and the volume of credit in circulation while maintaining a constant average price of goods, together with the elimination of any legal cover.

The main virus of the system as I see it is the almost unlimited freedom on the labour market, together with the extraordinary means of production. To produce the current requirements one is far from making use of the full available labour force. Therefore, there is unemployment and unhealthy competition among workers and both cause a reduction of the purchasing power and an unacceptable strangulation of all the economic blood stream.

What about the statement by the secretary of state for commonwealth relations, published in the Toronto Telegram of September 17, 1962, which reads as follows:
While Australia and New Zealand were practical and helpful in looking for means of improving common market conditions to the commonwealth, Canada was uncompromising.

Great Britain's purpose is quite clear. If she succeeds in associating with Europe, that will only strengthen the free world and help to offset the communist empire.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-24, to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a very simple bill. It would put into the Senate and House of Commons Act as a new subsection the following words:
No person who is a director of a company incorporated under the Companies Act or under any other public general act of Canada, or incorporated by a local or private act of Canada, shall be eligible to be a member of the Queen's privy council for Canada and a minister of the crown.
When I had the privilege of introducing this bill on October 1 I said by way of explanation that the effect of the bill is to establish by law what is now recognized in practice. As hon. members know, it has long been a subject of concern that two things
Senate and House of Commons Act be maintained, (1) the independence of parliament and (2) the avoidance of conflict of interest. There are a number of provisions in the Senate and House of Commons Act and in other pieces of legislation which aim to secure the independence of parliament and the independence of members of parliament from undue influences. But we also recognize that it is important that so far as cabinet ministers are concerned there be no conflict of interest between their public responsibilities and any private duties or obligations.
During the regimes of the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King and the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent there was considerable interest in this subject. It is well known that both of these former prime ministers requested members who joined their cabinets to relinquish directorships of companies in so far as it was possible, but he did not require them to do so. It is a matter of record-this can be found by consulting various sessional papers that were brought down a number of times in response to motions of mine-that most members of the cabinet of the last two prime ministers who had directorships resigned them on becoming members of those cabinets. However, this was not in those days a universal practice. During the last few years of the late Liberal government there was an outstanding case of a minister of that cabinet holding the directorship of a company, and many of us on the floor of the house felt there was a conflict of interest. We endeavoured to persuade the government of that day that that minister should either resign from the cabinet or resign his directorship. We did not win the point at that time, but at any rate the public did come to realize that the point we were making was valid.
I have to say quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, that the present Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) seems to have accepted this contention. Naturally, we outside the cabinet do not know all the secrets of what goes on inside the cabinet; we do not even know the secrets involved in getting appointments to the cabinet. But it is our general and public understanding that the present Prime Minister requires of anyone who would become a member of his cabinet that he resign any directorships he has. I understand, for example, that one of the most recent appointees to the cabinet-who does not happen to have a seat in this House of Commons-resigned a long list of such directorships and did so before he became a member of the cabinet. I placed on the order paper not long ago a series of questions similar to questions I put on the order paper in previous years, to which answers were given that make it
