Senate and House of Commons Act clear that no member of the present cabinet is, or has been since becoming a member of the cabinet, a director of any company as defined in the new subclause which I think should be written into the Senate and House of Commons Act.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is not necessary for me to argue for the acceptance of the principle contained in this bill, as I had to do when the Liberal government was in power and had in the cabinet at least one minister who was a director of a company. But it seems to me that now that this has been accepted as a recognized principle of practice we should write it into the law. I suggest that this is in the same category as the requirement that members of parliament shall not hold any office of emolument under the crown, or that members of parliament, whether they are private members or cabinet ministers, shall not be involved in any business relations with the government. As I say, Mr. Speaker, there are a number of other requirements of that nature protecting the independence of parliament. I think this same procedure should now be followed with regard to the position of cabinet ministers. As I have already said, I do not have to argue with this present government that cabinet ministers should not be directors; the present Prime Minister has accepted that. But it seems to me we should write into the law what is now practice, and we should make it clear that any future government, no matter what party it might be, will have to continue the practice that is now being followed.
I do not know whether the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) in the remarks he made just before five o'clock in another debate was seeking to set the stage for the discussion of my bill. At any rate, some of the remarks he made at that time were certainly relevant to my suggestion that it would be a good idea now to make this kind of protection for the future. I am free to admit that, so far as I am concerned this bill of mine does not go far enough. Men can resign from directorships in companies and corporations and still have a fairly strong personal interest in those companies. However, I do not yet know of any way, so long as we have the present kind of economic system, by which we can compel these men to divest themselves completely of their connections, although it is a fact that in the United States the law goes much further than is the case with respect to this bill.
In that connection may I say this. We feel that the affairs of our country should be run by people with the interests of the country at heart, and that this situation will come about only when we have a government made up of people drawn from all walks of


life, particularly with representatives of the working people, the farmers, the consumers and those engaged at the ordinary level in the life of our country. I may say quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, that is why some of us have tried to organize in this country the kind of party of which we in this corner are members and for whose progress we are working for all we are worth. However, under conditions as they are it seems to me that this is perhaps as far as we can ask this house to go. However, we certainly feel that the house should go at least this far.
I therefore have pleasure, Mr. Speaker, in moving the second reading of this bill the effect of which would be to provide that no directors of Canadian companies shall be eligible as ministers of the crown. In view of the fact that this is the practice now being followed by the government I dare to hope that the government might accept and support this bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. W. Baldwin (Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I doubt that anyone in the house would quarrel with the principle which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has sought to clothe with legal words in order to make it effective. However, the point on which I find myself in most agreement with him is when he says he had to admit he had experienced the utmost difficulty in attempting, if I might paraphrase his words, to find a legal bill or a legal vehicle which would carry forward into actual practice the thought which he has expressed. I wish to deal with the bill on a technical basis. I am going to deal with it on broader principle later on.
On the technical wording of the amendment which is proposed by this bill I think prima facie there are certain obvious defects which must appear to those who examine it. It reads as follows:
No person who is a director of a company incorporated under the Companies Act or under any other public general act of Canada, or incorporated by a local or private act of Canada, shall be eligible to be a member of the Queen's privy council for Canada and a minister of the crown.
I refer particularly to these last lines, "to be a member of the Queen's privy council for Canada and a minister of the crown". I am assuming that, in order to be a minister of the crown, you must be a member of the Queen's privy council and that these are interchangeable words. If that is so, while the word "and"-and I hope the hon. member is following me-is usually conjunctive, I wonder if it would have that interpretation here. I suggest that the words "a member of the Queen's privy council" must be regarded as surplusage

unless the word "and" is interpreted to mean "or". I can take no other meaning from it. If this be the case you would then have this situation, and this is the sort of thing which arises when legislation of this kind is drafted to serve a purpose and is subjected to the attacks which most legislation at one time or another is at least considered to be eligible for. You would have a situation where there are, I think, according to the last returns, approximately 86 or 87 members of the Queen's privy council, including those who are ministers of the crown. If this amendment has the meaning I take it to have, or could very easily have, you would then have a situation where those who were at one time ministers of the crown and have ceased to be such, or those who have been appointed for other reasons- and there are some very distinguished names which appear on this list-would come under the sanctions of this particular amendment. For example, I notice the name of a former prime minister, namely Mr. St. Laurent and Hon. Robert Winters who obviously, or at least apparently, are not now interested in the public life of this country. I use the word "apparently" with deliberation.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
speechtext:
As I say, this is begging the question. You go back to what would be considered to be a reasonable interpretation. I submit that it is quite reasonable for the word "and" to be construed as "or" in this particular case. If I am correct in this suggestion, then a member of the Queen's privy council but not a minister of the crown would be subject to the provisions of this bill.
Then there is a restriction, of course, as there necessarily must be, to a company incorporated under the local or private acts of Canada or public general acts of Canada. I do not know whether there could be an evasion. I am considering the matter. Quite possibly there could be an evasion of the spirit of the principle which the hon. member has in mind by being a director of a provincial company, a situation which might still bring up this question of conflict of interest just as frequently and just as substantially as if the minister of the crown were a director of a company incorporated under an act of Canada.
Senate and House of Commons Act This would rule out those who might hold directorships in companies incorporated under an act of Canada and of a charitable or community nature. I am not in a position to indicate whether there are or might be any. However, I think it is quite conceivable that the board wording which the hon. member has seen fit to use here could prevent people of that description from being a minister of the crown.
Before I go on to deal with the larger aspects of the proposition and to give my views as to why I do not think this particular amendment will serve the purpose which the hon. member has in mind, I think I should put on the record the position which has been taken by this government. The hon. member was good enough to refer to it. I think we can go back prior to 1959. In the debates of 1956, as recorded at page 5539, I find there was at that time a debate which took place in connection with the review of the estimates of the Department of Defence Production. The point at issue there was whether or not Mr. Howe, because of his position as an executor of the estate of Sir James Dunn, was in a position where the conflict of interest principle applied. I notice these comments by the Prime Minister on June 29, 1956, as found on page 5539 of Hansard:
I began by a reference that I believe summarizes the general attitude of parliaments in the British tradition to the need for ministers of the crown at all times to act in such a way that their conduct is in keeping with the proprieties of parliamentary traditions, and also in their conduct at all times to appear to keep within the limitations that the traditions of the past have imposed upon all who hold the high and honourable position of minister of the crown.
There then follows a quotation from a statement made by Sir Winston Churchill who at the time he made the statement was prime minister of the United Kingdom.
It is a principle of public life that ministers must so order their affairs that no conflict arises, or appears to arise, between their private interests and their public duties.
After the government changed in 1957 the principle which had been enunciated was repeated on at least two occasions by the right hon. gentleman who is now Prime Minister. I refer first to Hansard for 1960-61, page 6599, where the Prime Minister said in response to a question:
Mr. Speaker, the first act of the present government when it came into power was to ensure that no minister in the cabinet would hold a portfolio while at the same time having a position as a director of any company, whether public or private. That was to prevent the possibility of there being any connection between the award of contracts and the relationship of a minister to a company which might be in receipt of a contract.
I can only say in answer to the hon. member what I said the other day, that at no time did I ever hear directly or indirectly of anything which

Senate and House of Commons Act would have supported the suggestions that were made the other day during the course of the royal commission hearing. I can only say that we took measures we had advocated through the years, that ministers should not be connected in any way with corporations. That was a course we felt was necessary in order to preserve and maintain the integrity not only of ministers but also of the administration.
As found on page 7037 of Hansard for the same session the Prime Minister again answered a question in these words:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. gentleman answered his own question when he quoted what I said, namely that the ministers were asked to remove themselves as directors of companies. The hon. gentleman realizes that, as an eleemosynary or philanthropic organization, a hospital organization does not come within the category of companies. I am surprised that he is so shocked that the Parliamentary Guide so records the fact after the experience we had through the years of ministers of the crown being directors of companies that were dealing with the previous government.
That was the position being taken before this party formed the government and it was the consistent position adopted afterwards, a position which is not the same, as was mentioned by the Prime Minister, as that taken by the previous government. There is a noticeable distinction, and I find that nowhere is that better expressed than in two statements made by Mr. St. Laurent when as prime minister he was participating in a debate on May 12, 1955, and said, as found at page 3690 of Hansard, in response to a question asked by the present Prime Minister:
That is a matter about which I inquired before I became a member of the government, and I was told there was no rule of law or even traditional practice that required anyone who accepted such responsibilities to sever any previous connections he might have had. I was told that was something for each individual to consider in respect of his own position, and he might feel that it was desirable to sever all connections. In fact I felt that it was desirable to sever all such connections to avoid occasions for the kind of criticism-which I feel is not justified-
He referred to the criticism then being directed against one of the ministers. He later repeated this same comment and went on to say that this was a suggestion which had been made to him by Mr. Mackenzie King. I think there is a plain distinction there. The present Prime Minister has laid it down in the position he takes, which is consistent with that he took before 1957, that ministers of the crown should divest themselves of directorships. The position of the official opposition, as expressed in 1955 when they formed the government, was that this was something for each individual minister to consider according to his own views and the dictates of his own conscience.
There is another great error which I think has crept into the reasoning of the hon. member in his attempt to obtain adherence

to this principle by means of legislation. I have been engaged for a great many years in the study and practice of law, in fact since I began as a student at the age of 17. While it is essential and necessary from time to time to amend the law in order to try to obtain needed and necessary reforms and changes in legislation to meet the exigencies of the day, where there is, as in this country, an adherence to the common law system, a tradition of constitutional practice and an opportunity to build up a body of good, sound practice, I have come to the conclusion after all these years it is better to let this matter be dealt with in that way and to let it be molded and changed according to the changes in day to day and year to year requirements rather than embodying it in legislation which, as the hon. member has admitted, simply cannot meet the varying situations it must meet in order for his requirements to be completely served. I think this is a good illustration of this particular viewpoint.
There is a legal principle known to members of my profession that the mention of the one is the exclusion of the other. It seems to me that when the hon. member is attempting to incorporate this principle imperfectly in the form of legislation he is in effect saying that this matter will now be in statutory form, that within the statute will be contained the four corners of what he considers to be necessary to meet the problem of conflict of interest and that from now on nothing else goes. This is a very reasonable interpretation which could be made if this amendment to the Senate and House of Commons Act should become law. I think we would be left in that position.
It seems to me it is better to leave things as they are in view of the fact that the government has now adopted this principle. While I cannot offer any hope to hon. gentlemen opposite with respect to when they may cross the floor and occupy the positions of the government, I suppose that some day Liberals yet unborn will come here and form a Liberal government. But when this does happen I think they will then find enshrined and embodied in the constitutional practice of this country the system advocated and put into practice by the Prime Minister, and a principle which cannot then be altered. Having in mind the fact that you may have to envisage a situation where you would be dealing with more than just a directorship in which there might be a conflict of interest, I feel that this situation should be covered by our body of constitutional jurisprudence.
For example, in conducting a little research on this subject I find that in 1918, I believe it

was, there was an attempt to cover this situation. At that time a great many members of parliament were directors of companies which had engaged in contractual relationships with the government and some members felt something should be done to remedy the situation. A resolution was offered for the purpose of dealing with it. While there is, of course, a difference between an attempt to prevent a member of parliament from being a director and preventing a minister of the crown from being a director, nevertheless I read this to indicate to hon. members the type of language which was considered essential at that time to meet the situation.
The resolution was to disqualify any member during the time he is a director of or holds, either directly or indirectly, a controlling interest in any incorporated company from having a contract or agreement with the government, express or implied. Now, legislation framed in those words might come closer to meeting the situation, but it seems to me there could still be other combinations of facts which might give rise to a conflict of interests. It is my submission we have now made substantial progress towards covering the situation and I think the sensible thing to do would be to leave the matter open to become just as much a matter of constitutional practice as is responsible government.

In
rising to support this bill, I might point out that it is based on a well founded tradition of this house. The parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister (Mr. Baldwin) referred to an occurrence in 1918. I submit that one of the earliest and certainly one of the clearest opinions of the principle involved in this bill was once given by a prime minister of Great Britain nearly 50 years ago. The Right Hon. Herbert Asquith, speaking in the British House of Commons during a debate said, and I quote:
Ministers ought not to enter into any transaction whereby their private pecuniary interest might.
Senate and House of Commons Act
even conceivably, come into conflict with their public duty. . .Again, no minister is justified under any circumstances in using official information, information that has come to him as a minister, for his own private profit or for that of his friends .. . Again, no minister ought to accept from persons who are in negotiation with or seeking to enter into contractual or proprietary or pecuniary relations with the state any kind of favour.
Now, what the bill is attempting to achieve is to incorporate into the law a principle which is usually recognized in practice. I realize that there have been times when this practice, unfortunately, has been ignored. However, I think the principle of the bill is sound and I do not wish to prolong the debate unnecessarily because this would prevent the passage of timely legislation about which there should be no objection from any quarter of the house.
With all due respect to the parliamentary secretary, I may say that his chief objection to the bill is the reference to members of the privy council who are no longer members of parliament, and who may be affected. As a matter of fact, this bill does not envisage any such restrictions at all. I should like also to bring to the attention of this house a possible further application of this principle, one that has particular importance today because of the widespread personal financial interest in corporations with wide ramifications in almost every phase of industry and business.
All governments today are connected in one way or another with big business. The actions and decisions of the federal government have a continuing impact on all sectors of the economy. This is one factor that was not present when the rule pertaining to ministers having conflicting interest was originally drafted. At this point I should like to suggest a further development of this principle by providing that for a period of one year an ex-minister may not hold a directorship in a publicly owned corporation.
Any day now the Prime Minister may stumble across his February, 1958, dissolution speech and rediscover his conclusion that Canada cannot be governed very well by a minority government. If this happens, then presumably he will call an election. One result of that election conceivably might be that the 22 present cabinet ministers would find themselves without their ministerial responsibilities. No doubt they would find other work, and more lucrative work. Some of them might be asked to serve on the boards of corporations. By virtue of the fact they held positions as ministers of the crown they would naturally have gained knowledge that would be invaluable to the operation of industries of various types. These ex-ministers could use their acquired knowledge to the

Senate and House of Commons Act great advantage of the private corporations. It is with the possibility of this development in mind that I make the suggestion that the rule of obligation, as we now understand it and as it is embodied in this bill, be extended beyond the actual date when a minister ceases to hold a cabinet position and that he be barred from holding a directorship for a period of one year.
I should like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that I do not wish to imply present ministers would take advantage in any way of such a situation. Indeed, I do not wish to cast any reflection on any members of the present cabinet. Sir Winston Churchill, on February 25, 1952 as recorded on page 702 of the British Hansard, had this to say:
It is a principle of public life that ministers must so order their affairs that no conflict arises or appears to arise between their private interests and their public duties.
What I am suggesting, Mr. Speaker, is that this principle should apply for a reasonable period of time after a cabinet minister leaves office in order to avoid the appearance that his private interests are in conflict with his past public duties. This need not take legislative form but could become, rather, a part of the code of ethics which, although unwritten, governs the role of the executive under our parliamentary system.
This bill contains no controversial objectives. It is simply a confirmation of a practice which ministers generally have adhered to, and if approval of the bill will do away once and for all with possible situations embarrassing to this and future governments then I urge unanimous approval for it, and in so doing wish to commend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre for introducing it.

Mr. Speaker, I observe the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre attempting to try to close the debate, and I must say I sympathize with his effort, but we cannot proceed with this measure without giving it more careful examination. I feel that while in principle it is a very good bill there are a great many deficiencies in it. To begin with, the parliamentary secretary pointed out one of the difficulties, and that is in making an act of parliament or in defining a situation we sometimes lose the spirit of what is intended.
As the sponsor of the bill has said, the present government and members of the cabinet have resigned directorships and have carried out in effect the spirit of the bill; but it is open to question whether the bill as worded is broad enough to cover many of the situations that exist even now. I would like to mention some of these loopholes, so that the bill might be altered before it is passed.
The first and major problem I see is the lack of inclusion of provincially incorporated companies. The bill itself is quite clear that it can only apply to acts of the parliament of Canada; but most of the corporations operating within provinces are incorporated by provincial charter. Therefore the exclusion of directors of provincial corporations is a basic exclusion and to that extent the bill should be amended. It has a wide open clause which could easily be avoided by a person who is a director of a provincial company.
There are several other difficulties. As has already been pointed out, non-profit making corporations are also governed by directors, and they should also be covered. I do not think that directors of fraternal organizations and other such philanthropic corporations should be required to resign their directorships, and to that extent the term "director of a company" is too broad.
In addition to these generalities there are a good many ways by which an individual who wanted to get around the spirit of the bill could do so. There is no mention in it of the wives of directors, and the possibility of directorships being carried on in effect by the party involved but actually being in the name of his wife or a member of his family.
Another comparison should be made in connection with shareholders, and if we consider what happens in other countries we find that shareholders in large corporations which deal with governments are required to divest themselves of their shares before taking cabinet posts. This is particularly true

in the United States where many cabinet ministers have been shareholders in large motor corporations and have had to divest themselves completely of their shares, at very great personal loss, in order to take up duties as cabinet ministers. Whether or not the bill should be extended that far I am not prepared to say at the moment, but it is something that should be carefully considered.
Then there is always the possibility of a person holding stock in a company in trust, in the name of some other person, and there is also the situation of a director or shareholder in a controlling company which exercises control over a subsidiary. I am not suggesting that any ministers of the crown would adopt these methods I have mentioned in order to get around the provisions of the bill. It would be most unworthy of them and I would not expect it to happen; but my point is that in defining in very narrow terms what a cabinet minister shall do before assuming his cabinet post, we leave open a large number of things that probably should be included. I agree with the parliamentary secretary, that to legislate is not always in the best interests of securing results.

Since he seems to favour the principle of the bill but would like to see it improved, how would he like to agree to second reading being passed and the bill being referred to the committee on banking and commerce, of which he is the chairman, where he could play a very distinguished role in helping to improve it?

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will answer this by saying that I believe the bill is so basically deficient that it should be withdrawn and redrafted before we send it to the banking and commerce committee, or any other committee.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
speechtext: That is a reflection on the distinguished lawyer who drew it up.

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
speechtext:
I do not know who drew it up but I suspect that whoever drafted the bill did so in accordance with principles which were set forward. I am pointing out that the principles are not broad enough. The bill is open to misinterpretation and there are loopholes. The hon. member himself is an authority on the question of amendments. It seems to me the bill is so basically deficient that if we tried to amend the clauses we would find ourselves out of order. The bill includes only directorships in companies incorporated by act of Canada. If we are going to deal with this matter the bill should be redrafted before we even try to amend it.

The parliamentary secretary mentioned the wording of lines 11 and 12. He called attention to the inclusions of the word "and" in the phrase "a member of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada and a minister of the crown". I would agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that this is the type of change which might well be made in committee. If the words "who is" were substituted for the word "and" so that the phrase would read "a member of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada who is a minister of the crown" the matter would be more clear. If that were the only difficulty about this bill I would agree it might be worth sending to a committee where it could be further considered.
Another point I wish to raise concerns the fact that the words "directly or indirectly" are not used. I realize that many people who are not lawyers say lawyers are quibbling with words when they use such expressions as "directly or indirectly", but in this case I think it is important. A person can control a company without actually being a director. The words of some of the earlier statutes were probably more apt.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
speechtext: Is the hon. member suggesting that some of the members of the present cabinet who have resigned directorships are indirectly still controlling the companies with which they were connected?

subtopic: SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT
speechtext: I am not suggesting that. A moment ago I said I did not believe that any cabinet minister either in the past or in the future would be likely to resort to underhand methods of controlling a company where direct methods are prohibited. I am positive he would not do so. None the less, if we are asked to legislate we must legislate carefully. If certain words are used, those are the words which apply, and everything else is excluded. At present this is a question of trust. It is a question of the policy which has been laid down. If there is legislation, you have only the words to follow, not the spirit of the institution. For that reason I feel that the principle of the bill is deficient. It is deficient in its spirit and it is deficient in relation to the provincially incorporated companies.

speakeroldname: Mr. Thomas M. Bell (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice):

I was not sure that my hon. friend was going to give me an opportunity to speak, though I am anxious to take part in this debate. I agree 100 per cent with the thought behind this bill, but I would question whether it is necessary at the present time to set this principle in statutory form. I do, however, want to say that in my opinion the hon. member for Winnipeg

Senate and House of Commons Act North Centre deserves credit for continuing his efforts to bring this type of thing before parliament and the people.
I also believe we are fortunate in Canada that we have at the present time, as well as in the past, little difficulty about conflicts of interest such as have prevailed to some extent in the United Kingdom and in the United States. The parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister has expressed in an able way the legal disabilities which exist with regard to this bill. One of the thoughts he put on record was whether the bill in its reference to privy councillors would include all privy councillors or just those who are members of the cabinet.
When I look quickly through the record, one case which strikes me is the McCann controversy which arose in 1955. Information about this is to be found on page 6040 of volume 6 of Hansard for the 1955 session. I draw no conclusions from that brief controversy which concerned the then minister of national revenue, and I only mention it because of its interest in the light of the issue which has been raised by the parliamentary secretary this afternoon.
The present Prime Minister and the then leader of the opposition, Mr. Drew, were questioning the then prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, as to whether Dr. McCann, who was the minister of national revenue, had obtained certain tax information in his capacity as minister of national revenue or in his capacity as a director of the Guaranty Trust Company. Mr. St. Laurent refused to answer, saying that this was a matter of cabinet privilege. However, he invited Mr. Drew, who was a privy councillor, to come to him confidentially when the information would be made available to him. Mr. Drew declined, but I suggest that here is an instance where information of a cabinet nature might be available to other privy councillors who are not members of the cabinet, which would strengthen the argument of the parliamentary secretary that this bill should include all privy councillors if it were to be enacted.
Mr. Speaker, I see it is six o'clock. I merely add that I feel there is no need for this thought to be expressed in statutory form at the present time. I think we in Canada are very fortunate that our public men have never had any serious conflict, certainly since this government has been in office.

speakerposition: topic
Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since the house will be adjourned on Thursday next will the house leader give the business not only for Monday but for the rest of the week until the adjournment?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It is very difficult to outline the business for four days when we are not certain how much can be accomplished in any one day. We will of course have to finish interim supply in order that money will be available to carry on the normal duties. It would be followed by the national economic development board bill. Our hope, expressed some time ago, was that we could complete before the Christmas recess the national productivity council bill as well. Then there are three or four smaller matters which perhaps the house at the appropriate time would consider fairly rapidly. But we will wait until Monday evening to see what progress we make.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Would the house leader care to mention those small bills that he has in mind?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The ones I had in mind are these. There is the one under the heading of dominion-provincial tax rental agreements, which affects the universities and another small one dealing with sewage disposal projects. We might be able to bring before the house something with regard to the world's fair at Montreal. Then there is a railway bill dealing with the extension of a railway line in New Brunswick, which perhaps might be considered. These are smaller items which perhaps could be passed rather rapidly through the house. I would also like to bring before the house another subject that was mentioned earlier; that is the proposal to adjust the method of dealing with divorce bills in parliament. On Monday I will ask unanimous consent of the house to raise that particular bill to top place at five o'clock when private members' hour is reached.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: The house leader means Tuesday, does he not?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, five o'clock on Tuesday.
